inline.s: Aniruddha, in a former age, had been a robber. One night he came to a temple and saw the lamp before the Buddha about to go out. He drew an arrow and lifted the wick, and the lamp suddenly shone bright, its radiant light dazzling his eyes. Struck with awe, Aniruddha at once set aside evil and embraced the good. Evil after evil faded away, and every virtue came to full perfection, until at last he attained the fruit of realization.

In the Song dynasty Yang Zhonghe was a judicial officer of Xuzhou. During the Tiansheng era he was sent to Caizhou to hear a case, and because he made a wrongful judgment, the Northern Star registered its censure against him and he was to suffer a heavy punishment. Overcome with remorse and fear, Zhonghe at once gave up his post among the prisons of officialdom, vowing to cultivate a hundred good deeds to atone for his fault. Whenever he met itinerant monks and Daoists, the poor and lacking, widowers, widows, the orphaned and the childless, or those in mourning, sickness, or urgent need, he never failed to rescue and relieve them. Within a few years his household was left entirely empty, and morning and evening he attended only to the incense before the True Martial Lord. In the end, because of his courage in mending his faults, the True Lord took pity on him, appeared in the guise of a Daoist, and entrusted him with the spirit-tallies of the Twelve True Lords, bidding him to cultivate the Way. Later he was received into the register of the Eastern Peak and appointed as the recording clerk of Maxi; and the court posthumously honored him as the Realized One Who Awakened to the Source. Ming Chao Qizong commented: “Of the six lines of the Qian hexagram, the later ones speak of good fortune and the earlier ones of being without blame, and of having regret. One who can feel regret can mend his faults and so arrive at good fortune. How great is the meaning of regret!” Ming Chen Liangmo also said: “A person’s poverty or wealth, honor or disgrace, longevity or early death — even down to a single meal, a single word, one action or one rest — all have their fixed reckonings, which nothing can resist. Yet the pivot by which fortune and misfortune turn lies with the person, and the reckoning cannot hem him in. For the fixed reckoning is the mandate of Heaven, while the sympathetic response is the Mind of Heaven. Heaven takes as its very heart the giving of life, and is utterly sincere and without deceit. If a person’s single thought to help others and benefit creatures issues from the depth of his being, and is at first done with no deliberate aim, then though it be but one moment and one affair, when his sincerity reaches its utmost it can reach up and move the Mind of Heaven, and the answer comes as an echo answers a sound. This is the necessary working of principle. The reckoning is the reckoning of Heaven. Once the Mind of Heaven is moved, the reckoning turns along with it — how could it confine him? Consider the punishments, rewards, and statutes of a state, which, once fixed, are not to be changed. Yet if a minister can truly move his sovereign’s heart through his loyalty and sincerity, then one who has been banished may be summoned back, and one on the point of execution may receive a pardon; in an instant joy and anger are wholly reversed. How can any of this not be changed? From this we know that principle and reckoning contend with and yield to each other, and that the deeds of hidden virtue and of responsive influence in ancient and modern times stand out clearly and are not false.”
(Mr. Yu Quyuan, following the ancient text, struck out the two words “three years.”)

This section sums up the entire treatise and in truth teaches people the path of following the good and forsaking evil. The word therefore carries forward and refers to all that has gone before. The “auspicious person” is one who, because he does good, is able to obtain fortune; the “inauspicious person” is one who, because he does evil, is able to bring upon himself doom. The many evils and the many virtues can never be exhausted; but if one seeks their substance, they fall into three categories — speech, sight, and action — and these are precisely the place where one should lay hold in earnest. Good in speech means refraining from speaking what is contrary to propriety, delighting in praising others’ good, and arousing the good heart of others. Good in sight means refraining from looking at what is contrary to propriety, delighting in seeing good people, delighting in reading good books, ever beholding one’s own faults and never marking another’s failings. Good in action means refraining from moving contrary to propriety, never treading what is unlawful, doing good bravely and eagerly, at all times making things convenient for others, in every way accumulating hidden merit, leading and inducing one’s own region and even the farthest reaches, transforming and stirring those of like mind, and sharing the good with all people. Evil is the opposite of all this. Three years means a thousand days — the method of assessing merit used in the reigns of Tang and Yu, and the time of fulfillment, when good is piled up and evil is filled to the brim. The human heart is exceedingly alive and changes without constancy; if for the term of three years the heart does not shift, then its good or evil has become pure. The text here singles out the word Heaven — the great lord who rewards good and punishes evil, who grants fortune and sends down calamity, and the converging point of the whole treatise. Yet Heaven is my own heart. Mencius says: “Preserve the heart and nourish the nature, and so serve Heaven.” The two word “must” do not refer to the dark, vast, soundless and odorless heavens above; they refer to the words, sights, and actions of these three years as they issue from my own heart. “What is asked for one gets not from another but from oneself” — this is the principle. The perfected person delights in the Way and does not originally seek fortune; to do good in order to seek fortune is for the heart to have already lapsed into selfishness. Therefore one should only do fully what lies in one’s own power and receive what Heaven bestows, without the slightest thought of covetous expecting or fawning entreaty. Yet because the mind summons things to itself and Heaven’s way returns recompense, the principle of fortune and misfortune, which fills the heavens and floods the earth and misses nothing in the veriest detail, is so. The people of the world who regard doing good and forsaking evil as the business proper to themselves are certainly of the very highest among the high. But the world abounds in ordinary folk; how can they all be of superior faculties? Hence those who stand in awe of misfortune and seek fortune, and who forsake evil and do good, are also the very hope of the Supreme One — precisely because he fears that people will not seek fortune. “In seeking there is a Way; in obtaining there is a mandate,” and to seek in this way profits the obtaining. To seek in this way harms nothing in the seeking. “Bestowing fortune” means such things as enjoying fortune and emolument in one’s own person, having virtuous and sons, honor and splendor and greatness, a lengthened span of life, a thriving household, and harmony in all affairs — extending even to becoming a sage or worthy, an immortal or a Buddha, fully awakening to one’s own nature, directly realizing the Unborn, delivering people and creatures, and setting a model for ten thousand generations. “Sending down calamity” means such things as suffering conspicuous disaster in one’s own person, having wicked and dangerous sons, decline and ruin and downfall, a shortened allotment of years, the ruin of the household, obstruction in every affair — extending even to dying and entering the Avici hell, transmigrating among other species, enduring suffering through endless kalpas, bequeathing a stream of evil to later generations, and being cursed through ten thousand years. Alas! Judging from this, the way of fortune and misfortune is great indeed — truly beyond thought and speech! The final clause sets forth effort in practice, speaking only of “practicing all the good,” which is the one master-key of the whole treatise. The word effort (mian) is the most essential method for moving to good and mending one’s faults. It is not a word of sighing wonder. Practice (xing) is to put it into effect with one’s own body. To practice with effort is to strive and exert oneself, never turning back even to death. The Book of History says: “It is not knowing that is hard, but doing.” The proverb says: “A foot of talk is not worth an inch of walking.” If one knows yet does not act, one will surely gain nothing from it; and gaining nothing, one cannot but go on into the sea of birth and death to reap what one has sown. Those in the world who would seek a path of life must put forth the effort of death. Zhu Xi said: “When the yang breath rises, even metal and stone are pierced through; where the spirit reaches, what task is not accomplished?” If people can do this, then their practice is full and their merit complete, and they become true and realize sagehood — is this not what may surely be attained?

Now that no good is without fortune and no evil is without calamity is the constant of Heaven’s way. And the retribution of good and evil falls in some cases on one’s own person, and in some cases on one’s descendants. There are the wicked of this present life whose merit from a former life has ripened, so that though they ought to suffer calamity they instead receive fortune; and the virtuous of this present life whose guilt from a former life has ripened, so that though they ought to receive fortune they instead suffer calamity. Only after the fortune and calamity of the preceding life have been exhausted does the retribution of good and evil in this life fall upon them one by one. This is merely a matter of sooner or later, of first and last; it does not mean that the retribution of good and evil is ever forfeited. Therefore it is said: “The laws of the visible world are swift and may be escaped; the statutes of the unseen are slow and never miss. The net of the visible is wide and easy to slip through; the net of the unseen is fine and hard to flee.” Now the people of today, having done a single good deed, at once expect their reward, and if a thing goes a little against them they say Heaven’s way is hard to know. But do they not know that so long as one is neither hungry nor cold, free of disaster and harm, so that the scholar can read, the farmer can till, the artisan can work, and the merchant can trade, now opening one’s mouth in a smile and rarely furrowing one’s brow — where is this not the happiness of peace and safety? Were this not so, the world’s desires are boundless and the world itself is flawed; how could everyone be rich, honored, and successful? The people of the world should only revere and trust the Record of Response and Practice, and give themselves to it as occasion arises; then naturally their fortune and emolument will be immeasurable and their descendants honored and flourishing. Practice it for one year and ten thousand offenses are wiped out; practice it for four years and a hundred blessings gather; practice it for seven years and one’s descendants pass the examinations; practice it for ten years and one’s years are lengthened; practice it for fifteen years and everything goes as one wishes; practice it for twenty or thirty years and one’s name is written in the registers of the immortals; practice it for fifty years and the heavenly spirits show reverence, and one takes his seat in the higher worlds. These are the true, un-deceiving words of the Supreme One; the only fear is that people will not put them into practice. By and large, one who aims at the great Way, from the moment of his vow, undertakes to deliver himself and deliver others. To deliver oneself and deliver others lies above all in cultivating both fortune and wisdom. To cultivate wisdom one must see one’s nature and clarify one’s own school; to cultivate fortune one must observe the five constant virtues and the hundred good works. When these two are joined in harmony, the Supreme God will await him with a mandate of Heaven, and the Buddhas will surely draw him into the Pure Land. Not only will he transcend to the higher worlds, but in truth he will suddenly realize the Unborn, beyond birth and death; and then he may enter the world to deliver beings and resolve this one great matter of cause and conditions. If one merely seeks a long life and cultivates the vital nature — that is what is called not cultivating samadhi: when the reward is spent one returns, and even if one is born in the heaven of neither-thinking-nor-not-thinking, with a life of eighty-four thousand great kalpas, in the end one is scattered again into the various realms and cannot escape the world. And these various realms all arise because one has not understood the wondrous bright mind; from delusion they accumulate, and delusion gives rise to the three worlds, within which delusion sinks and drowns through the seven destinies. Because karmic influences summon one, each follows its own kind. But if one fully awakens to bodhi, these deluded conditions originally have no existence at all; and the power of his universal gateway practice is sufficient to sustain him. Hence one who can resolve this great matter of cause and conditions must return to the Two Blessings and the Two Perfections.

The Perfected One Qiyun (Wang Zhi) said in his Discourse at Panshan: Someone asked, “How can one get beyond the retribution of crime and fortune?” The master said: “Crime, fortune, cause, and effect belong to the shell of yin and yang. If you can get out of the shell of yin and yang, then there is no crime or fortune, no cause or effect. What is the shell of yin and yang? Whenever in your heart there is the slightest thought of selfish desire and self-interest, that belongs to the yin shell; whenever there is the slightest thought of delight in doing good, that belongs to the yang shell. In yin there is the retribution of evil; in yang there is the retribution of good. If you can refine the substance of your mind to emptiness, neither good nor evil, with not a hair’s breadth of obstruction, and be master of yourself, then fortune and calamity cannot lay hold upon you, and cause and effect cannot entangle you. This is a true man who has escaped the shell of yin and yang.”

Zhu Hui'an (Xi) of the Song dynasty practiced the rules of conduct with great strictness, which the later scholars found inconvenient. They did not realize that in an age when the principle of learning was not yet clear and people were casting about in their minds and guessing at their natures, the very rootfulness that loosed men from restraint and loathed all machinery lay hidden here. Had not Zhu Xi upheld it for a while, it would long since have burst apart. At that time the Way of Learning was proscribed and false learning was registered in the guilt lists, pointing to it as an evil air. Among the noisy multitude were the buffoons of Han Tuozhou, the partisan enmity of Lin Li, the bitter grievances of Wang Huai and Chen Jia. The Six Classics and Confucius and Mencius were made a great prohibition of the age; “rightness of heart and sincerity of will” were things the court loathed to hear. The scholars who walked within the square and the compass drew in their breath and held their tongues, while those who ran to the fire and bent soft in the wind usurped the names of other masters. Xi alone carried the lineage of the Way upon his shoulders, without fear and without quaking. He set forth the writings of the classics, sparing no book; he drew forward men of talent without a single idle day. His memorials and sealed letters cut to the very bone and pierced to the heart. His community granaries and relief measures rescued the burning and saved the drowning. In matters of advance and retreat he never took a single step carelessly; under slander and defamation he stood a hundredfold unshaken. In adorning later scholars, many worthy men vied to come forth; in strictness toward himself, the four prohibitions he never transgressed. Therefore the learning of Zou, Lu, Lian, and Luo rose like the sun in mid-heaven — the sure effect of Zhu Xi’s earnest practice.

Fan Yan of the Song dynasty, a man of Renzhou, in the prime of life passed the highest examination with honors, and went through posts from commandery and county up to minister and counselor, holding office for more than twenty years. Every day he pondered how to be loyal to his sovereign and benefit the people; in seeing, hearing, speaking, and acting he did not dare to be in the least careless. Even in a dark room or in the hidden corner of a leaking house he always wore an aspect of trembling vigilance and self-admonition. When his sons were grown, he at once gave up office and retired, wearing coarse cloth and eating plain food, having no dealings with the affairs of the world. With a pure mind he entered the Way, and daily recited the Lotus and Prajna sutras; in his leisure he practiced meditation and contemplation, not retaining the slightest particle of worldly truth. Even his moral nature and his life-mandate he let return to the natural. By the Daguang era, at over ninety, he suddenly had an awakening. He instructed his attendant: “To live in this world is like a stage play — when the gongs and drums sound, the scholar, the beauties, the clown, and the villain each display their arts; and when the candle is burnt out and the lamp is gone, what savor remains? So, too, have I come into this world for ninety years, like an illusion, like a transformation, like dew, like lightning. Happily I have wakened to this — and this has no boundary or shore, no square or round, no size; not red or white, blue or yellow; no long or short, no high or low; no anger, no joy; no right, no wrong; no good, no evil. It is what is called: not a single thing is there, yet a myriad images are all contained. This is the most real and most supreme, the subtle principle that comes not and goes not. It lies only in one’s utmost sincerity and diligence, heart following heart without break, thought continuing without end. The Buddhas of the three times all issue from this place. This is called true speech, real speech, thus speech — not lying speech, not divergent speech. Each of you should strive to practice it.” When he had spoken, he sat silently, palms together, and passed away. At once a rare fragrance filled the room, auspicious clouds spread through the sky, and all manner of radiance illuminated the world, not dispersing for several days. Ten thousand eyes looked up together in awe. As to the items already set forth above, they are the practice of the Way of the three teachings, ascending from lower learning to higher comprehension, and returning together to the exhausting of principle and the perfecting of nature, to the very ultimate of the mandate. I have recorded them here as the highest standard for those who practice the threefold conduct. Let him who has aspirations ponder them!

Zhang Gongchen said: “All doing, without exception, begins from the small and grows to the great. Hence every creature that has blood and breath may directly realize the supreme bodhi. But this supreme bodhi lies only in guarding the minute and being watchful when alone, and in expanding it ever further. Did not Master Yuan say, ‘The past of every kind is like dying yesterday; the future of every kind is like being born today’? How can one abandon and ruin oneself, laying all fortune and calamity at the feet of Heaven’s mandate, drifting on and wandering, and so end this one life? Having already taken refuge in the gate of Buddhism, I shall not shrink from repeating myself a few times more at the end of this chapter, hoping that all who have roots of goodness may avail themselves of it to broaden themselves.”

The world is supremely vast and ten thousand generations supremely distant; even with ten thousand hands and ten thousand eyes to succor this present world, it would still not be enough. Therefore the most urgent matter is only to teach people. Surely one does not have to be a sage or worthy before he can teach others! If a person truly delights at hearing of good, rejoices at seeing good, ever recounts good words, speaks of good deeds, tells of good retribution, and distributes good books — then he has already done much teaching. In the midst of this the turning is subtle, the workings quick and alive, and there is a place where it advances further and refines further, until at last it attains to transformation and accommodation without one’s knowing it. And to teach the common man is not as good as to teach the hero: get one such man, and he may turn heaven and reverse earth, guard what the ancients handed down and await the future, so that men teach men in turn, and teaching becomes universal teaching. The sages and worthies of old, whose classics and books have been handed down through the ages, all fulfilled this one great matter of cause and conditions. This present chapter is the profound commentary of the Supreme One for delivering the world, and the secret principle of all the Buddhas for saving living beings. Benevolent indeed this wondrous making, giving birth without end! All who recite it, practice it, engrave it, and transmit it also share in this one great matter of cause and conditions. To awaken the age and open the eyes of the people, to nurture the source and bring forth fortune, to join with others in goodness, the heavens and earth grow pure and serene. The capacity of one mind, in kalpas without number, ever full — truly it passes all thought!

blocks.text: Postface to the Re-engraved Record of Response and Practice

inline.s: When I first obtained the Record of Response and Practice Compendium, its cover was already falling off, and the preface by Minister Peng Zhiting survived in half a page. The scripture proper had eight lines to the page, fourteen characters to the line, and a preface by Wu Shengzhai of Xiqiao, dated the plum month of the xin chou year of Qianlong; but it did not reach the name of the compiler, saying only: “Now this precious compendium, with its sentences punctuated and its sections explained, section by section and verse by verse.” It further said: “Behold, these pear and jujube blocks are re-engraved.” From this it appears that this was a reprint. Later, in the study of my uncle Cheng Yunhe, I saw another copy, whose cover likewise bore no compiler’s name nor the place of the stored blocks. The scripture proper had eight lines to the page and twenty-six characters to the line, with ten blank pages at the head and no preface — evidently a copy printed just as the first engraving was finished, intended to be sent about to beg for prefaces. Now that I have this copy, the scripture is also in small characters and the cover says the blocks are kept at the Yao residence south of Guocao Bridge in the palace lane of Suzhou; the finest paper was chosen and ink-printed, and the cost is reckoned at eighty-two wen per copy for paper and print, plus twenty-five wen for the cloth wrapper. This is the actual price, and fearing it might be increased they did not put it on the market. That is fifty characters there. The Peng preface says: “Chen, a student of our countryside, gathered a company of scholars, trimmed the old edition, and compiled it into one book.” Under the date of the plum month of xin chou in the Wu preface there are further the eighteen characters: “On an auspicious dawn, the disciple who received and upheld it, Wu Jiazu, respectfully inscribed; Chen Gengxin respectfully engraved.” Whether Wu Jiazu is the same as Wu Xiqiao, and whether Chen Gengxin is the same as Master Chen, I cannot tell. Considering that the Peng preface speaks of “Master Chen the scholar” who compiled the book, he seems to belong to the latter time; yet to make him a man of former times would serve as well. Now the compendium records the honor paid to Lu Qingxian for his place in the Confucian temple, and Lu Qingxian was so honored in the fourth year of Yongzheng; this book was printed in the forty-sixth year of Qianlong. Therefore Master Chen must be a man of that latter time. And if he is a man of the latter time, then this copy is a first printing. But even so, to make him a man of the early Qianlong years is not impossible either; while this copy is itself a reprint. Yet whether first printing or second, why should the blocks not have remained with the Chen and Wu families but have been kept in the Yao residence? Can it be that the blocks passed into the hands of the Yao family and that too at a later time? These are all things that can no longer be ascertained. When I went to Caozhao to inquire for the Yao family, they were already vanished, and none of the old folk of the neighborhood knew any longer where these blocks might be. At the end of the compendium it says, “I have already taken refuge in the gate of Buddhism” — this is the very man who presided over and compiled this book. This gentleman’s eye and hand are exceedingly high; my judgment is that his headings and notes are the preface, and the commentary at the end of each section is the postface. Why need he compose another preface or introduction? What matters is only that the book be entirely good and entirely beautiful, looking toward the deliverance of people and the world; and as for the name of the compiler who gathered it and those who supplied it, there is no need to preserve it. By my reckoning, since the Zhao and Song dynasties the commentators on the Record of Response have numbered several hundred schools, and of those surviving today there are several dozen kinds. Of all that I have seen, none surpasses the Compendium and the Plain Exposition. The Plain Exposition, since the ren chen year of Daoguang, has been re-engraved by my fellow townsman Liu Zigang and has again obtained circulation. Now, upon re-engraving the Compendium, the blocks are finished and stored at Shilin temple within the city of Suzhou, west of Dongjing bridge outside the Changmen gate, and printed at the studio of Wu Qingxia. My earnest wish is that those whose strength is small may ask for a single copy to read and recite, and that those whose strength is ample may have it printed and distributed far and wide. In former times a clerk of the unseen world told Zhou Chi: “If this scripture is upheld in one region, that region is spared distress; if upheld in all the world, then all the world is at peace and prosperous.” A friend of mine, seeing these four lines, said that the benefit could not be so great and that the words were overstated. Alas! If you could but explain these four lines clearly, you would trust of yourself that the words are true and certain and contain not the slightest exaggeration. The recipient is like a partner receiving his wages — his share by right, with nothing to decline, and nothing to be wanting. The upholder is like a woman who loves her jewels — fearing only to lose them and ever guarding against damage. These are merely shallow similes. The Doctrine of the Mean says, “Having obtained one good, clasp it to the breast and never lose it” — this is the meaning of “receiving and upholding.” The scripture proper says: “Commit no evil; practice all the good. The auspicious person is good in speech, good in sight, good in action; if in one day he has three goods, then within three years if near, or within one life if far, this is the method of receiving and upholding.” The “one region” is the people of one region, each one so receiving and upholding. The scripture goes on: “When the mind rises in good, the auspicious spirits already follow it” — how much more when within one region all the people receive and uphold it, for a long time and again a long time! How could there be any who do not turn calamity to fortune and encounter peril to become auspicious? In old times when Huang Chao rose in rebellion and slaughtered all under heaven, he was about to pass through the village of filial Cai; he gave the order, “To alarm a filial son is to forfeit the aid of Heaven; who harms a single blade of grass or tree of the region where a filial son dwells shall be put to death without pardon.” He gathered his troops and passed by, not violating a hair of it. This is one man’s receiving and upholding sheltering a whole region, and the people of the region being able to receive his influence — one region that received and upheld and so escaped distress. Again, the inhabitants of Chaozhou had done evil so long that the Supreme God commanded the whole city to sink and become a lake; only the household of the Jia family, being good, moved the Realized True Martial Lord to manifest his transformation and direct them to flee to a distance. This is one region suffering disaster while one family alone escaped. Let me add one word more: “If one man receives and upholds this book, one man is delivered; if one household receives and upholds it, one household is at peace.” For if a man can receive and uphold this book, he will make honor and disgrace equal, reduce gain and loss to the same, awaken to the illusion of transformation, and understand clearly the principle of the rise and fall of prosperity; and so he can pass his days according to circumstances without being stained by worldly conditions. Is this not one man receiving and upholding, one man alone obtaining deliverance? As for a household in which there are roots of goodness from the past, naturally they blend like water and milk, and are transformed without the labor of the tongue. Is this not one household receiving and upholding, one household at peace? And if among them there be those who have old blessings of a former life but no wisdom, who once entered the womb became wholly blind, though they got human form yet their karmic obstacles are deep and heavy and they are on the point of falling — such are as the deaf and the blind, and will never believe. The Earth Store Sutra says, “The power of karmic hindrance is great; it can obstruct the holy path.” This is its meaning. How can one not fear it? How can one not strive?
